nodes.name: Space R(S) of type-preserving representations of the once-punctured torus group
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a once-punctured torus and let $R(S)$ be the space of conjugacy classes of representations $\rho:\pi_1(S) \to {\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)$ which takes a loop surrounding the cusp to a parabolic element.

nodes.name: Space AH(S) of Kleinian punctured torus groups
nodes.statement: The space $AH(S)$ of Kleinian punctured torus groups is the subset of $R(S)$ of faithful representations with discrete images.

nodes.name: AH(S) self-bumps and is not locally connected (McMullen; Bromberg)
nodes.statement: For example, McMullen \cite{Mc2} showed that $AH(S)$ self-bumps, and Bromberg \cite{Br} showed that $AH(S)$ is not even locally connected.
conclusions: $AH(S)$ self-bumps
$AH(S)$ is not even locally connected

nodes.name: Convergence of linear slices to the Maskit slice
nodes.statement: It is natural to ask the following question: ``When $\beta$ tends to $2$, does $\mathcal L(\beta)$ converge to $\mathcal L(2)$?"
nodes.statement_short: Does the linear slice L(beta) converge to the Maskit slice L(2) as beta tends to 2?

nodes.name: Parker-Parkkonen convergence of real linear slices
nodes.statement: Parker and Parkkonen \cite{PP} studied this question in the case that a real number $\beta>2$ tends to $2$, and obtained an affirmative answer for this case.
nodes.statement_short: For real beta>2 tending to 2, the linear slices converge to the Maskit slice.

nodes.name: Convergence of linear slices: horocyclic vs tangential
nodes.statement: Suppose that a sequence $\beta_n \in \mathbb C \setminus [-2,2]$ converges to $2$. If $\beta_n \to 2$ horocyclically, then $\mathcal L(\beta_n)$ converge to $\mathcal L(2)$ in the sense of Hausdorff. On the other hand, if $\beta_n \to 2$ tangentially, then $\mathcal L(\beta_n)$ converge (up to subsequence) to a proper subset of $\mathcal L(2)$ in the sense of Hausdorff.
conclusions: $\mathcal L(\beta_n)$ converge to $\mathcal L(2)$ in the sense of Hausdorff

nodes.statement_short: Linear slices converge to the Maskit slice under horocyclic convergence of the trace, but to a proper subset under tangential convergence.

nodes.name: Sketch of the tangential case of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement: We now sketch the essential idea which is underlying this phenomenon. Especially we explain the reason why the limit of linear slices is a proper subset of $\mathcal L(2)$ in the case where $\beta_n \to 2$ tangentially. Now suppose that $\beta_n \to 2$ tangentially, and that a sequence $\alpha_n \in \mathcal L(\beta_n)$ converges to $\alpha \in \mathbb C$. We will explain that $\alpha$ should lie in a proper subset of $\mathcal L(2)$. Let us take a sequence $\rho_n \in AH(S)$ such that $({\mathrm{tr}} \,\rho_n(a),{\mathrm{tr}}\,\rho_n(b))=(\alpha_n,\beta_n)$. Since $(\alpha_n, \beta_n) \to (\alpha,2)$ as $n \to \infty$, and since $AH(S)$ is closed, we have $(\alpha,2) \in AH(S)$, and hence $\alpha \in \mathcal L(2)$. By taking conjugations, we may assume that $\rho_n(a) \to A_\alpha$ and $\rho_n(b) \to B$ in ${\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)$, where $$ A_\alpha=\left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha & -i \\ -i & 0 \end{array}\right) \quad \text{and} \quad B=\left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array}\right). $$ In addition, by pass to a subsequence if necessary, we may also assume that the sequence $\rho_n(\pi_1(S))$ converges geometrically to a Kleinian group $\Gamma$, which contains the algebraic limit $\langle A_\alpha, B\rangle$. From the assumption that $\beta_n \to 2$ tangentially, one can see that the cyclic groups $\langle\rho_n(b) \rangle$ converge geometrically to rank-$2$ abelian group $\langle B, C \rangle$, where $C$ is of the form $$ C=\left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & \zeta\\ 0 & 1 \end{array}\right) $$ for some $\zeta \in \mathbb C \setminus \mathbb R$, see Theorem \ref{cyclic}. Therefore the geometric limit $\Gamma$ contains the group $\langle A_\alpha,B, C\rangle$. For any given integer $k$, one see from $C^{k} A_\alpha=A_{\alpha-k i\zeta}$ that the group $\langle A_{\alpha-ki\zeta}, B\rangle$ is a subgroup of the Kleinian group $\Gamma$. Hence the group $\langle A_{\alpha-ki\zeta}, B\rangle$ is discrete and thus $\alpha -ki\zeta \in \mathcal L(2)$. Therefore $\alpha$ should be contained in the intersection $$ \bigcap_{k\in \mathbb Z} (k i\zeta+\mathcal L(2)), $$ which is a proper subset of $\mathcal L(2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: a tangential geometric limit contains an extra parabolic C, so alpha - k i zeta lies in L(2) for all k, forcing alpha into a proper subset.

nodes.name: Paired manifold
nodes.statement: Let $(M, P)$ be a paired manifold; that is, $M$ is a compact, hyperbolizable $3$-manifold with boundary and $P$ is a disjoint union of tori and annuli in $\partial M$. Especially, every torus component of $\partial M$ is contained in $P$.
nodes.genus: $M$ is a compact, hyperbolizable  $3$-manifold with boundary
differentia: $P$ is a disjoint union of tori and annuli in $\partial M$

nodes.name: Set of type-preserving irreducible representations
nodes.statement: Let $$ {\cal R}(M,P):={\mathrm{Hom}}_P^\mathrm{irr} (\pi_1(M),{\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)) $$ denote the set of all type-preserving, irreducible representations of $\pi_1(M)$ into ${\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)$.

nodes.name: Type-preserving representation
nodes.statement: Here a representation $\rho: \pi_1(M) \to {\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)$ is said to be {\it type-preserving} if $\rho(\gamma)$ is parabolic or identity for every $\gamma \in \pi_1(P)$.

nodes.name: Space of representations R(M,P)
nodes.statement: The space of representations $$ R(M,P):={\cal R}(M,P)/{\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C) $$ is the set of all ${\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)$-conjugacy classes $[\rho]$ of representations $\rho$ in ${\cal R}(M,P)$.

nodes.name: Algebraic topology on R(M,P)
nodes.statement: We endow this space $R(M,P)$ with the algebraic topology; that is, a sequence $[\rho_n]$ converges to $[\rho]$ if there are representatives $\rho_n$ in $[\rho_n]$ and $\rho$ in $[\rho]$ such that for every $g \in \pi_1(M)$ the sequence $\rho_n(g)$ converges to $\rho(g)$ in ${\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)$.

nodes.name: Space AH(M,P) of faithful discrete representations
nodes.statement: We are interested in the topological nature of the space $$ AH(M,P):=\{\rho \in R(M,P) : \rho \text{ is faithful, discrete}\}. $$

nodes.name: Closedness of AH (Jorgensen)
nodes.statement: It is known by J{\o}rgensen \cite{Jo} that $AH(M,P)$ is closed in $R(M,P)$.
conclusions: $AH(M,P)$ is closed in $R(M,P)$

nodes.name: Minimally parabolic geometrically finite representations MP(M,P)
nodes.statement: Let $MP(M,P)$ denote the subset of $AH(N,P)$ consists of representations $\rho$ which are minimally parabolic (i.e., $\rho(g)$ is parabolic if and only if $g \in \pi_1(P)$) and geometrically finite.

nodes.name: Interior of AH (Marden, Sullivan)
nodes.statement: It is known by Marden \cite{Mar} and Sullivan \cite{Su} that $MP(N,P)$ is equal to the interior of $AH(N,P)$ as a subset of $R(N,P)$.

nodes.name: Density theorem (Brock-Canary-Minsky)
nodes.statement: Recently, it was shown by Brock, Canary and Minsky \cite{BCM} that the closure of $MP(M,P)$ is equal to $AH(M,P)$.

nodes.name: Once-punctured torus S
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a torus with one open disk removed.

nodes.name: Generators a, b of pi_1(S)
nodes.statement: Throughout of this paper, we fix a pair $a,b$ of generators of $\pi_1(S)$ such that the geometric intersection number equals one.

nodes.name: Paired manifold (N,P)
nodes.statement: Now we set $$ N:=S \times [0,1] $$ and $$ P:=\partial S \times [0,1]. $$

nodes.name: Paired manifold (N,P')
nodes.statement: We next set $P':=P \cup A$, where $A \subset S \times \{1\}$ is an annulus whose core curve is freely homotopic to $b \in \pi_1(S)$.

nodes.name: Paired manifold (N-hat, P-hat)
nodes.statement: Finally, we let \begin{eqnarray*} ({\hat N},{\hat P}):=(N \setminus W, P \cup T), \end{eqnarray*} where $W$ is a regular tubular neighborhood of $b \times \{1/2\}$ in $N=S \times [0,1]$ and $T:=\partial W$.
nodes.statement_short: Drill a tubular neighborhood W of b x {1/2} out of N and add its boundary torus T to the parabolic locus.

nodes.name: AH(N,P') lies in the boundary of AH(N,P)
nodes.statement: Note that $AH(N,P')$ lies in the boundary of $AH(N,P)$; in fact $\rho \in AH(N,P)$ lies in $AH(N,P')$ if and only if $\rho(b)$ is parabolic.

nodes.name: Maskit slice
nodes.statement: This space $AH(N,P')$ is called the {\it Maskit slice} of $AH(N,P)$.

nodes.name: R(N,P) as representations with commutator trace -2
nodes.statement: In this case, the space $R(N,P)$ consists of all ${\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)$-conjugacy classes of representations $$ \rho: \pi_1(S)=\langle a,b \rangle \to {\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C) $$ which satisfy the condition ${\mathrm{tr}} (\rho([a,b]))=-2$.

nodes.name: Trace pair determines the representation up to b -> b^{-1}
nodes.statement: As we will see below, for any given $(\alpha,\beta) \in \mathbb C^2$, there is a representation $\rho \in R(N,P)$ which satisfies ${\mathrm{tr}}^2\rho(a)=\alpha^2, \, {\mathrm{tr}}^2\rho(b)=\beta^2$, and this $\rho$ is determined uniquely up to pre-composition of automorphism $(a,b) \mapsto (a,b^{-1})$ of $\pi_1(N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Every (alpha,beta) is realized by a representation with these squared traces, unique up to the automorphism (a,b)->(a,b^{-1}).

nodes.name: Trace domain D_tr
nodes.statement: Therefore the subset $$ \mathcal D_{{\mathrm{tr}}}:=\{(\alpha,\beta) \in \mathbb C^2 : \exists \rho \in AH(N,P) \text{ s.t. } {\mathrm{tr}}^2\rho(a)=\alpha^2, \, {\mathrm{tr}}^2\rho(b)=\beta^2\} $$ of $\mathbb C^2$ is well-defined.
nodes.statement_short: D_tr = pairs (alpha,beta) realized as squared traces of a and b by some representation in AH(N,P).

nodes.name: Symmetry of D_tr
nodes.statement: Note that the set $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{tr}}$ is symmetric under the action $(\alpha,\beta) \mapsto (\beta,\alpha)$.

nodes.name: Linear slice
nodes.statement: For a given $\beta \in \mathbb C$, the slice $$ \mathcal L(\beta):=\{\alpha \in \mathbb C : (\alpha,\beta) \in \mathcal D_{{\mathrm{tr}}}\}. $$ of $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{tr}}$ is called the {\it linear slice} for $\beta$.
also_stated_at: More precisely, we consider in this paper the shape the {\it linear slice} $$ \mathcal L(\beta):=\{\alpha \in \mathbb C : (\alpha,\beta) \in AH(S)\} $$ of $AH(S)$ when $\beta$ close to $2$.

nodes.name: Symmetry of linear slices
nodes.statement: Note that $\mathcal L(\beta)$ is symmetric under the action of $z \mapsto -z$.

nodes.name: Representation rho_alpha in R(N,P')
nodes.statement: For a given $\alpha \in \mathbb C$, let $\rho_\alpha$ be the representation in $R(N,P')$ defined by $$ \rho_\alpha(a):= \left(\begin{array}{cc} \alpha & -i \\ -i & 0 \end{array}\right), \quad \rho_\alpha(b):= \left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 2 \\ 0& 1 \end{array}\right). $$

nodes.name: Parametrization of R(N,P') by C
nodes.statement: The map $\psi:\mathbb C \to R(N,P')$ defined by $\alpha \mapsto \rho_\alpha$ is a homeomorphism.
conclusions: The map $\psi:\mathbb C \to R(N,P')$ defined by $\alpha \mapsto \rho_\alpha$ is a homeomorphism
nodes.label: trace2

nodes.name: psi maps L(2) onto the Maskit slice
nodes.statement: Note that the map $\psi$ in Lemma \ref{trace2} induces a homeomorphism from $\mathcal L(2)$ onto the Maskit slice $AH(N,P')$.

nodes.name: Existence of trace coordinates
nodes.statement: There exist an open, connected, simply connected domain $\Omega \subset R(N,P)$ and a homeomorphism $$ {\mathrm{Tr}}:\Omega \to \mathbb C^2 $$ which satisfy the following: \begin{enumerate} \item $\Omega$ contains $R(N,P')$, and ${\mathrm{Tr}}$ takes $R(N,P')$ onto $\mathbb C \times \{2\}$. In addition, we have ${\mathrm{Tr}}(\rho_\alpha)=(\alpha,2)$ for every $\alpha \in \mathbb C$. \item For every $\rho \in \Omega$, ${\mathrm{Tr}}(\rho)=(\alpha,\beta)$ satisfies ${\mathrm{tr}}^2 \rho(a)=\alpha^2$ and ${\mathrm{tr}}^2 \rho(b)=\beta^2$. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: $\Omega$ contains $R(N,P')$, and ${\mathrm{Tr}}$ takes $R(N,P')$ onto $\mathbb C \times \{2\}$
we have ${\mathrm{Tr}}(\rho_\alpha)=(\alpha,2)$ for every $\alpha \in \mathbb C$
For every $\rho \in \Omega$, ${\mathrm{Tr}}(\rho)=(\alpha,\beta)$ satisfies ${\mathrm{tr}}^2 \rho(a)=\alpha^2$ and ${\mathrm{tr}}^2 \rho(b)=\beta^2$
nodes.statement_short: A simply connected domain Omega containing R(N,P') carries a homeomorphism Tr to C^2 recording the traces of a and b, with R(N,P') sent to C x {2}.
nodes.label: trace

nodes.name: Trace coordinates
nodes.statement: We call ${\mathrm{Tr}}$ the {\it trace coordinate map} and $(\alpha,\beta)={\mathrm{Tr}}(\rho)$ the {\it trace coordinates} of $\rho \in \Omega$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.4
nodes.statement: We only need to show that the orbit of $ \theta(\Delta)$ under the action of $\mathbb Z_2 \times \mathbb Z_2$ on $\Xi$ are mutually disjoint. Take two points $(\alpha,\beta), (\alpha',\beta') \in \Delta$. Suppose for contradiction that $(\alpha,\beta, \gamma(\alpha,\beta)), (\alpha',\beta',\gamma(\alpha',\beta')) \in\Xi $ are equivalent under the action of non-trivial element of the covering transformation group $\mathbb Z_2 \times \mathbb Z_2$. Since $\mathrm{Re}\,\beta>0$ and $\mathrm{Re}\,\beta'>0$, one see that $(\alpha',\beta',\gamma(\alpha',\beta'))=(-\alpha,\beta, -\gamma(\alpha,\beta))$. Then from (3.1) we have \begin{eqnarray*} \gamma(\alpha',\beta')&=&\frac{1}{2}\left( \alpha' \beta' + \sqrt{\alpha'^2\beta'^2-4(\alpha'^2+\beta'^2)}\right) \\ &=&\frac{1}{2}\left( -\alpha \beta + \sqrt{\alpha^2\beta^2-4(\alpha^2+\beta^2)}\right). \end{eqnarray*} But this with $\gamma(\alpha',\beta')=-\gamma(\alpha,\beta)$ implies $\sqrt{\alpha^2\beta^2-4(\alpha^2+\beta^2)}=0$, which contradicts to $(\alpha,\beta) \in \Delta$.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: two points identified by a covering transformation would force the square root to vanish, impossible on Delta.

nodes.name: Reduce to disjointness of the Z2xZ2-orbits of theta(Delta)
nodes.statement: We only need to show that the orbit of $ \theta(\Delta)$ under the action of $\mathbb Z_2 \times \mathbb Z_2$ on $\Xi$ are mutually disjoint.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to disjointness of the Z2xZ2-orbits of theta(Delta)

nodes.name: Assume two points of theta(Delta) are equivalent
nodes.statement: Take two points $(\alpha,\beta), (\alpha',\beta') \in \Delta$. Suppose for contradiction that $(\alpha,\beta, \gamma(\alpha,\beta)), (\alpha',\beta',\gamma(\alpha',\beta')) \in\Xi $ are equivalent under the action of non-trivial element of the covering transformation group $\mathbb Z_2 \times \mathbb Z_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume two points of theta(Delta) are equivalent

nodes.name: Re beta>0 forces the sign pattern
nodes.statement: Since $\mathrm{Re}\,\beta>0$ and $\mathrm{Re}\,\beta'>0$, one see that $(\alpha',\beta',\gamma(\alpha',\beta'))=(-\alpha,\beta, -\gamma(\alpha,\beta))$. Then from (3.1) we have \begin{eqnarray*} \gamma(\alpha',\beta')&=&\frac{1}{2}\left( \alpha' \beta' + \sqrt{\alpha'^2\beta'^2-4(\alpha'^2+\beta'^2)}\right) \\ &=&\frac{1}{2}\left( -\alpha \beta + \sqrt{\alpha^2\beta^2-4(\alpha^2+\beta^2)}\right). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Re beta>0 forces the sign pattern; compute gamma via (3.1)

nodes.name: The square root would vanish, contradicting the choice of De
nodes.statement: But this with $\gamma(\alpha',\beta')=-\gamma(\alpha,\beta)$ implies $\sqrt{\alpha^2\beta^2-4(\alpha^2+\beta^2)}=0$, which contradicts to $(\alpha,\beta) \in \Delta$.
nodes.statement_short: The square root would vanish, contradicting the choice of Delta

nodes.name: Commutative diagram of trace maps
nodes.statement: \xymatrix{ \widetilde R(N,P) \ar[d]^\pi \ar[r]^{\quad \widetilde {\mathrm{Tr}}} & \Xi \\ \quad \quad R(N,P) \supset \Omega \ar[r]^{\quad \quad \quad {\mathrm{Tr}}} & \Delta. \ar[u]_\theta }

nodes.name: Pass to the SL(2,C) representation space
nodes.statement: To show Lemma \ref{trace}, it is convenient to consider the space $\widetilde R(N,P)$ of representations of $\pi_1(N)$ into ${\mathrm{SL}}(2,\mathbb C)$, instead of ${\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)$. More precisely, the set $\widetilde R(N,P)$ consists of ${\mathrm{SL}}(2,\mathbb C)$-conjugacy classes of representations $\tilde \rho$ of $\pi_1(S)$ into ${\mathrm{SL}}(2,\mathbb C)$ which satisfy the condition ${\mathrm{tr}} (\tilde\rho([a,b]))=-2$. The ${\mathrm{SL}}(2,\mathbb C)$-conjugacy class of $\tilde \rho$ is also denoted by $\tilde \rho$ if there is no confusion.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the SL(2,C) representation space

nodes.name: Recall the trace-triple parametrization (Lemma 3.3)
nodes.statement: It is well known that an element $\tilde \rho$ of $\widetilde R(N,P)$ is uniquely determined by the triple $({\mathrm{tr}}\tilde \rho(a),{\mathrm{tr}}\tilde \rho(b),{\mathrm{tr}}\tilde \rho(ab))$ of complex number (see for example \cite{Bo} or \cite{Go}): \begin{lem} The map $$ \widetilde {\mathrm{Tr}}: \widetilde R(N,P) \to \Xi:=\{(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) \in \mathbb C^3 : \alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=\alpha\beta\gamma\} \setminus \{(0,0,0)\} $$ defined by $\tilde\rho \mapsto ({\mathrm{tr}}\tilde \rho(a),{\mathrm{tr}}\tilde \rho(b),{\mathrm{tr}}\tilde \rho(ab))$ is a homeomorphism. \end{lem}
nodes.statement_short: Recall the trace-triple parametrization (Lemma 3.3)

nodes.name: Solve for gamma: projection Pi is a 2-to-1 branched cover
nodes.statement: By using this lemma, we often identify $\widetilde R(N,P)$ with the subset $\Xi$ of $\mathbb C^3$. For $(\alpha,\beta) \in \mathbb C^2$, the numbers $\gamma$ satisfying $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=\alpha\beta\gamma$ are given by \begin{equation*} \gamma=\frac{1}{2}\left( \alpha \beta \pm \sqrt{\alpha^2\beta^2-4(\alpha^2+\beta^2)} \right). \end{equation*} Therefore the projection $$ \Pi:\Xi \to \mathbb C^2 \setminus\{(0,0)\} $$ defined by $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) \mapsto (\alpha,\beta)$ is a two-to-one branched covering map.
nodes.statement_short: Solve for gamma: projection Pi is a 2-to-1 branched cover

nodes.name: Trace identity tr(AB)+tr(AB^{-1})=trA trB identifies the two
nodes.statement: If we denote by $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ the solutions of the equation $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=\alpha\beta\gamma$ on $\gamma$, we have $\gamma_1+\gamma_2=\alpha\beta$. On the other hand, we have $$ {\mathrm{tr}} (AB)+{\mathrm{tr}}(AB^{-1})={\mathrm{tr}} A \, {\mathrm{tr}} B $$ for every $A,B \in {\mathrm{SL}}(2,\mathbb C)$. Therefore one see that if two representations $\tilde \rho_1, \tilde \rho_2$ in $\widetilde R(N,P)$ have the same image under the map $\Pi \circ \widetilde {\mathrm{Tr}}$, they are only differing by pre-composition of the automorphism $(a,b) \mapsto (a,b^{-1})$ of $\pi_1(S)$.
nodes.statement_short: Trace identity tr(AB)+tr(AB^{-1})=trA trB identifies the two lifts

nodes.name: Covering map pi with deck group Z2xZ2
nodes.statement: Now let $$ \pi:\widetilde R(N,P) \to R(N,P) $$ be the natural projection, which is a four-to-one covering map. The group of covering transformation for $\pi$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z_2 \times \mathbb Z_2$ which is generated by $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) \mapsto (-\alpha,\beta, -\gamma)$ and $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) \mapsto (\alpha,-\beta,-\gamma)$, where $\widetilde R(N,P)$ is identified with $\Xi \subset \mathbb C^3$ as in Lemma \ref{Bow}.
nodes.statement_short: Covering map pi with deck group Z2xZ2

nodes.name: Choose the domain Delta avoiding critical values
nodes.statement: Now let us take an open, connected and simply connected domain $\Delta \subset \mathbb C^2 \setminus\{(0,0)\}$ which satisfy the following: \begin{enumerate} \item $\Delta$ contains the set $\mathbb C \times \{2\}$, and \item $\Delta$ lies in the set $\{(\alpha,\beta) \in \mathbb C^2 : \mathrm{Re}\, \beta>0,\, \alpha^2\beta^2\ne 4(\alpha^2+\beta^2)\}$. \end{enumerate} Here, the condition $\alpha^2\beta^2\ne 4(\alpha^2+\beta^2)$ is equivalent to the condition that the pair $(\alpha,\beta)$ is not a critical value of the projection $\Pi:\Xi \to \mathbb C^2 \setminus \{(0,0)\}$. Throughout of this paper, we fix such a domain $\Delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose the domain Delta avoiding critical values

nodes.name: Choose the branch of the square root, giving theta
nodes.statement: Since $\alpha^2\beta^2\ne 4(\alpha^2+\beta^2)$ for every $(\alpha,\beta) \in \Delta$, and since $\Delta$ is connected and simply connected, one can take a univalent branch of the square root of $\alpha^2\beta^2- 4(\alpha^2+\beta^2)$ on $\Delta$. We take the branch such that the value for $(\alpha,2) \in \Delta$ is equal to $-4i$. Then we obtain the univalent branch of \begin{eqnarray} \gamma=\gamma(\alpha,\beta)=\frac{1}{2}\left( \alpha \beta + \sqrt{\alpha^2\beta^2-4(\alpha^2+\beta^2)}\right) \end{eqnarray} on $\Delta$, and hence the univalent branch $\theta: \Delta \to \Xi$ of $\Pi^{-1}$ on $\Delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose the branch of the square root, giving theta

nodes.name: Inner Lemma 3.4 and its proof
nodes.statement: \begin{lem} The map $ \pi \circ \widetilde {\mathrm{Tr}}^{-1} \circ \theta:\Delta \to R(N,P) $ is a homeomorphism onto its image. \end{lem} \begin{proof} We only need to show that the orbit of $ \theta(\Delta)$ under the action of $\mathbb Z_2 \times \mathbb Z_2$ on $\Xi$ are mutually disjoint. Take two points $(\alpha,\beta), (\alpha',\beta') \in \Delta$. Suppose for contradiction that $(\alpha,\beta, \gamma(\alpha,\beta)), (\alpha',\beta',\gamma(\alpha',\beta')) \in\Xi $ are equivalent under the action of non-trivial element of the covering transformation group $\mathbb Z_2 \times \mathbb Z_2$. Since $\mathrm{Re}\,\beta>0$ and $\mathrm{Re}\,\beta'>0$, one see that $(\alpha',\beta',\gamma(\alpha',\beta'))=(-\alpha,\beta, -\gamma(\alpha,\beta))$. Then from (3.1) we have \begin{eqnarray*} \gamma(\alpha',\beta')&=&\frac{1}{2}\left( \alpha' \beta' + \sqrt{\alpha'^2\beta'^2-4(\alpha'^2+\beta'^2)}\right) \\ &=&\frac{1}{2}\left( -\alpha \beta + \sqrt{\alpha^2\beta^2-4(\alpha^2+\beta^2)}\right). \end{eqnarray*} But this with $\gamma(\alpha',\beta')=-\gamma(\alpha,\beta)$ implies $\sqrt{\alpha^2\beta^2-4(\alpha^2+\beta^2)}=0$, which contradicts to $(\alpha,\beta) \in \Delta$. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Inner Lemma 3.4 and its proof

nodes.name: Define Omega and Tr
nodes.statement: Now let $$\Omega:=\pi \circ \widetilde {\mathrm{Tr}}^{-1} \circ \theta(\Delta)$$ and $$ {\mathrm{Tr}}:=\left(\pi \circ \widetilde {\mathrm{Tr}}^{-1} \circ \theta\right)^{-1}:\Omega \to \Delta. $$ Then we obtain the following commutative diagram: \begin{eqnarray} \xymatrix{ \widetilde R(N,P) \ar[d]^\pi \ar[r]^{\quad \widetilde {\mathrm{Tr}}} & \Xi \\ \quad \quad R(N,P) \supset \Omega \ar[r]^{\quad \quad \quad {\mathrm{Tr}}} & \Delta. \ar[u]_\theta } \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Define Omega and Tr; commutative diagram (3.2)

nodes.name: Check Tr(rho_alpha)=(alpha,2) from the branch choice
nodes.statement: To show that this $\Omega$ and ${\mathrm{Tr}}$ satisfy the desired property in Lemma \ref{trace}, we only need to show that ${\mathrm{Tr}}(\rho_\alpha)=(\alpha,2)$ for every $\alpha \in \mathbb C$. This can be seen from the following two facts: (i) If we regard $\rho_\alpha=\psi(\alpha)$ as an element of $\widetilde R(N,P)$, we have $\widetilde {\mathrm{Tr}}(\rho_\alpha)=(\alpha,2,\alpha-2i)$. (ii) From our choice of the branch $\theta$, we have $\theta(\alpha,2)=(\alpha,2 , \alpha-2i)$. Thus we complete the proof of Lemma \ref{trace}.
nodes.statement_short: Check Tr(rho_alpha)=(alpha,2) from the branch choice

nodes.name: Reduce to Tr(rho_alpha)=(alpha,2)
nodes.statement: To show that this $\Omega$ and ${\mathrm{Tr}}$ satisfy the desired property in Lemma \ref{trace}, we only need to show that ${\mathrm{Tr}}(\rho_\alpha)=(\alpha,2)$ for every $\alpha \in \mathbb C$. This can be seen from the following two facts:
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Tr(rho_alpha)=(alpha,2)

nodes.name: Fact (i): trace triple of rho_alpha
nodes.statement: (i) If we regard $\rho_\alpha=\psi(\alpha)$ as an element of $\widetilde R(N,P)$, we have $\widetilde {\mathrm{Tr}}(\rho_\alpha)=(\alpha,2,\alpha-2i)$.
nodes.statement_short: Fact (i): trace triple of rho_alpha

nodes.name: Fact (ii): branch theta matches, concluding the lemma
nodes.statement: (ii) From our choice of the branch $\theta$, we have $\theta(\alpha,2)=(\alpha,2 , \alpha-2i)$. Thus we complete the proof of Lemma \ref{trace}.
nodes.statement_short: Fact (ii): branch theta matches, concluding the lemma

nodes.name: Representation sigma_mu
nodes.statement: Given $\mu \in \mathbb C$, we define a representation $\sigma_\mu \in R(N,P')$ by \begin{eqnarray*} \sigma_{\mu}(a):=\left(\begin{array}{cc} -i\mu & -i \\ -i & 0 \end{array}\right), \quad \sigma_{\mu}(b):=\left(\begin{array}{cc} 1& 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array}\right). \end{eqnarray*}

nodes.name: Maskit slice M (in mu-coordinate)
nodes.statement: The subset $$ \mathcal M:=\{\mu \in \mathbb C : \sigma_\mu \in AH(N,P')\} $$ of $\mathbb C$ is also called the {\it Maskit slice}.

nodes.name: M is homeomorphic to the Maskit slice
nodes.statement: Since that the map $\mathbb C \to R(N,P')$ defined by $\mu \mapsto \sigma_\mu$ is a homeomorphism from Lemma \ref{trace2}, $\mathcal M$ is homeomorphic to $AH(N,P')$, and the interior $\mathrm{int}(\mathcal M)$ of $\mathcal M$ is homeomorphic to $MP(N,P')$.

nodes.name: L(2) = iM
nodes.statement: Since $\mu \in \mathcal M$ if and only if $-i\mu \in \mathcal L(2)$, we have $$ \mathcal L(2)=i\mathcal M=\{i \mu : \mu \in \mathcal M\}. $$
conclusions: \mathcal L(2)=i\mathcal M=\{i \mu : \mu \in \mathcal M\}

nodes.name: Translation invariance of M
nodes.statement: Note that $\mathcal M$ is invariant under the translation $\mu \mapsto \mu+2$.

nodes.name: Two components of the Maskit slice (Minsky)
nodes.statement: It is known by Minsky (Theorem B in \cite{Mi}) that $\mathcal M$ has two connected components $\mathcal M^+, \,\mathcal M^-$, where $\mathcal M^+$ contained in the upper half-plane and $\mathcal M^-$ is the complex conjugation of $\mathcal M^+$
also_stated_at: It is known by Minsky \cite{Mi} that $AH(N,P')$ has exactly two connected components.

nodes.name: Fundamental group of N-hat and the meridian c
nodes.statement: The fundamental group of ${\hat N}$ is expressed as $$ \pi_1(\hat N)=\langle a,b,c : [b,c]=\mathit{id}\rangle, $$ where $a,b$ is the pair of generators of the fundamental group of $S \times \{0\} \subset {\hat N}$, and $c$ is freely homotopic to an essential simple closed curve on $T$ that bounds a disk in $W$.

nodes.name: Representation sigma-hat_{mu,zeta}
nodes.statement: For a given $(\mu,\zeta) \in \mathbb C^2$, we define a representation $\hat\sigma_{\mu,\zeta} \in R({\hat N},{\hat P})$ by \begin{eqnarray*} \hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(a):=\sigma_\mu(a), \quad \hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(b):=\sigma_\mu(b), \quad \hat\sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(c):=\left(\begin{array}{cc} 1& \zeta \\ 0 & 1 \end{array}\right). \end{eqnarray*}

nodes.name: Parametrization of R(N-hat,P-hat) by C^2
nodes.statement: The map $\mathbb C^2 \to R({\hat N},{\hat P})$ defined by $(\mu,\zeta) \mapsto \hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}$ is a homeomorphism.

nodes.name: Notation for sigma-hat
nodes.statement: Following the rule of notation in \cite{Br}, the representation $\hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}$ should be written as $\sigma_{\mu,\zeta}$. But we reserve the notation $\sigma_{\mu,\zeta}$ for another representation, which will be defined in the next subsection.

nodes.name: Set B
nodes.statement: We define a subset $\mathcal B$ of $\mathbb C^2$ by \begin{eqnarray*} \mathcal B:=\{(\mu,\zeta) \in \mathbb C^2 : \hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta} \in AH({\hat N},{\hat P})\}. \end{eqnarray*}

nodes.name: B is homeomorphic to AH(N-hat,P-hat)
nodes.statement: Then, by the above lemma, the map $$\mathcal B \to AH({\hat N},{\hat P})$$ defined by $(\mu,\zeta) \mapsto \hat\sigma_{\mu,\zeta}$ is a homeomorphism.

nodes.name: (mu,zeta) in B implies mu in M
nodes.statement: Note that $(\mu,\zeta) \in \mathcal B$ implies $\mu \in \mathcal M$ since the restriction of $\hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}$ to the subgroup ${\langle a, b\rangle}$ of $\pi_1({\hat N})$ is equal to $\sigma_\mu$.

nodes.name: Real zeta is excluded from B
nodes.statement: Note also that if $\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta=0$ then $(\mu,\zeta) \not\in\mathcal B$; in fact, if $\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta=0$, it violates discreteness or faithfulness of the representation $\hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}$.

nodes.name: Points of B give translates in M
nodes.statement: Since $$ \hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(c^{-k}a)= \left(\begin{array}{cc} -i(\mu-k\zeta)& -i \\ -i & 0 \end{array}\right) \quad \text{and} \quad \hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(b)= \left(\begin{array}{cc} 1& 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array}\right), $$ one can see that if $(\mu,\zeta) \in \mathcal B$ then $\mu -k\zeta \in \mathcal M$ for every $k \in \mathbb Z$.
conclusions: $\mu -k\zeta \in \mathcal M$ for every $k \in \mathbb Z$

nodes.name: Bromberg's characterization of B
nodes.statement: Let $(\mu,\zeta) \in \mathbb C^2$ with $\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta \ne 0$. Then $(\mu,\zeta) \in \mathcal B$ if and only if $\mu -k\zeta \in \mathcal M$ for every integer $k$.
conclusions: $(\mu,\zeta) \in \mathcal B$ if and only if $\mu -k\zeta \in \mathcal M$ for every integer $k$
nodes.label: BromLem

nodes.name: Sets B^+ and A
nodes.statement: Now let $$ \mathcal B^+:=\{(\mu,\zeta) \in \mathcal B: \mathrm{Im}\,\zeta>0\} $$ and define a set $\mathcal A \subset \mathbb C \times \hat {\mathbb C}$ by $$ \mathcal A:=\mathcal B^+ \cup (\mathcal M \times \{\infty\}). $$

nodes.name: Bromberg's local model theorem
nodes.statement:
For any $
u \in \mathrm{int}(\mathcal M)$, there exist a neighborhood $U$ of $(
u,\infty)$ in $\mathcal A$, a neighborhood $V$ of $\sigma_
u$ in $AH(N,P)$, and a homeomorphism $ \Phi:U 	o V. $
conclusions: there exist a neighborhood $U$ of $(\nu,\infty)$ in $\mathcal A$, a neighborhood $V$ of $\sigma_\nu$ in $AH(N,P)$,  and a homeomorphism $ \Phi:U \to V.$
nodes.statement_short: Near each interior point of the Maskit slice, AH(N,P) is locally homeomorphic to the model set A.
nodes.label: BromThm

nodes.name: Bromberg's theorem for M^-
nodes.statement: Although Bromberg restricted to the case that $\nu \in \mathrm{int}(\mathcal M^+)$ in \cite{Br}, it is obvious that the same argument works well for $\nu \in \mathrm{int}(\mathcal M^-)$.

nodes.name: Bromberg's coordinates
nodes.statement: In this situation, we say that $(\mu,\zeta) \in U$ is {\it Bromberg's coordinates} of the representation $\Phi(\mu,\zeta) \in V$.

nodes.name: Notation sigma_{mu,zeta}
nodes.statement: In what follows, we also write $$ \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}:=\Phi(\mu,\zeta). $$

nodes.name: sigma_{mu,infty}
nodes.statement: If $\zeta=\infty$ then $\sigma_{\mu,\infty} $ is defined to be $\sigma_\mu$.

nodes.name: Quotient manifold M-hat_{mu,zeta}
nodes.statement: If $\zeta \ne \infty$, the quotient manifold $$ \hat M_{\mu,\zeta}={\bf H}^3/\hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(\pi_1({\hat N})) $$ has a rank-$2$ cusp whose monodromy group is generated by $\hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(b)$ and $\hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(c)$.

nodes.name: Filling theorem (Hodgson-Kerckhoff-Bromberg)
nodes.statement: Since we are choosing $U$ sufficiently small, it follows from the filling theorem due to Hodgson, Kerckhoff and Bromberg (see Theorem 2.5 in \cite{Br}) that there exists a {\it $c$-filling} $M_{\mu,\zeta}$ of $\hat M_{\mu,\zeta}$ for every $(\mu,\zeta) \in U$ with $\zeta \ne \infty$.

nodes.name: c-filling
nodes.statement: More precisely, there is a complete hyperbolic manifold $M_{\mu,\zeta}$ homeomorphic to the interior of $N$ and an embedding $$ \phi_{\mu,\zeta}:\hat M_{\mu,\zeta} \to M_{\mu,\zeta} $$ which satisfy the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item the image of $\phi_{\mu,\zeta}$ is equals to $M_{\mu,\zeta}$ minus the geodesic representative of $(\phi_{\mu,\zeta})_*(\hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(b))$, \item $(\phi_{\mu,\zeta})_*(\hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(c))$ is trivial in $\pi_1(M_{\mu,\zeta})$, and \item $\phi_{\mu,\zeta}$ extends to a conformal map between the conformal boundaries of $\hat M_{\mu,\zeta}$ and $M_{\mu,\zeta}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A c-filling is a complete hyperbolic manifold homeomorphic to int N with an embedding of M-hat missing exactly the core geodesic, killing c and conformal at infinity.

nodes.name: c-filling map
nodes.statement: The map $\phi_{\mu,\zeta}$ is called the {\it $c$-filling map}.

nodes.name: Construction of sigma_{mu,zeta}
nodes.statement: Then $\sigma_{\mu,\zeta}$ is defined to be a representation of $\pi_1(N)$ into ${\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)$ induced form $\phi_{\mu,\zeta} \circ \Pi_{\mu,\zeta} \circ f_\mu$; \begin{eqnarray*} \begin{CD} N@>{f_\mu}>{\text{marking}}> M_\mu @>{\Pi_{\mu,\zeta}}>{\text{covering}}> \hat M_{\mu,\zeta} @>{\phi_{\mu,\zeta}}>{\text{filling}}> M_{\mu,\zeta}. \end{CD} \end{eqnarray*}

nodes.name: sigma_{mu,zeta} is faithful
nodes.statement: This $\sigma_{\mu,\zeta}$ is faithful, and hence, is contained in $AH(N,P)$ (see Lemma 3.6 in \cite{Br}).

nodes.name: Complex length
nodes.statement: For any element $g \in {\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)$, its {\it complex length} $l(g) \in \mathbb C$ is a value which satisfies $$ {{\mathrm{tr}}^2 g}= 4\cosh^2 \left(\frac{l(g)}{2}\right). $$

nodes.name: Normalization domain Lambda
nodes.statement: For a loxodromic element $g \in {\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)$, its complex length $l(g)$ determined uniquely if we take it in the set $$ \Lambda:=\{z \in \mathbb C : \mathrm{Re} \,z > 0, \, -\pi< \mathrm{Im} \,z \le \pi\}. $$

nodes.name: Right half-plane C_+
nodes.statement: Note that the map $z \mapsto 2 \cosh(z/2)$ takes the interior of $\Lambda$ into the right-half plane $$\mathbb C_+:=\{z \in \mathbb C : \mathrm{Re}\,z>0\}.$$

nodes.name: Complex length map lambda
nodes.statement: We define a map $$ \lambda:\mathbb C_+ \setminus (0,2) \to \Lambda $$ as its inverse.
also_stated_at: Then the complex length $\lambda$ of $\rho(b)$ is determined by the relation $ \beta=2\cosh (\lambda/2) $ and the normalization $\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda>0,\,\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda \in (-\pi,\pi]$.

nodes.name: Asymptotics of lambda near 2
nodes.statement: Then we have \begin{eqnarray*} \lambda(z) &=&2\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac{z}{2}\right) \\ &=& 2 (z-2)^{1/2}+o(z-2) \quad (z \to 2), \end{eqnarray*} where the real part of a square root is chosen positive.

nodes.name: lambda(tr g) = l(g)
nodes.statement: We have $$\lambda({\mathrm{tr}}\, g)=l(g)$$ for every loxodromic element $g \in {\mathrm{SL}}(2,\mathbb C)$ with ${\mathrm{tr}} \,g \in \mathbb C_+ \setminus (0,2]$.

nodes.name: Main estimate: Bromberg vs trace coordinates
nodes.statement:
Let $
u \in \mathrm{int}(\mathcal M)$. For any $\epsilon>0$, we can choose a neighborhoods $U$ of $(
u,\infty)$ and $V$ of $\sigma_
u$ in Theorem ef{BromThm} so that they also satisfy the following: $V$ is contained in the domain $\Omega$ of the trace coordinate map, and for any $(\mu,\zeta) \in U$ with $\zeta 
e \infty$, we have  egin{enumerate} \item $|\mu-i\alpha| \le \epsilon$, and \item $|\zeta-4\pi i/\lambda( eta)| \le \epsilon \, \mathrm{Im}\,\zeta$, \end{enumerate} where $(\alpha, eta)={\mathrm{Tr}}(\sigma_{\mu,\zeta})$ is the trace coordinates of $\sigma_{\mu,\zeta}$
conclusions: $V$ is contained in the domain $\Omega$ of the trace coordinate map
$|\mu-i\alpha| \le \epsilon$
$|\zeta-4\pi i/\lambda(\beta)| \le \epsilon \, \mathrm{Im}\,\zeta$
nodes.statement_short: Near the Maskit slice, Bromberg's coordinates (mu,zeta) are approximated by (i alpha, 4 pi i / lambda(beta)) from the trace coordinates.
nodes.label: estimate

nodes.name: Origin of the estimates
nodes.statement: These estimates 1 and 2 follow from the fact that we can choose the $c$-filling map $\phi_{\mu,\zeta}:\hat M_{\mu,\zeta} \to M_{\mu,\zeta}$ close to the isometry outside a neighborhood of the rank-$2$ cusp. Then the estimates 1 and 2 are obtained from estimates due to McMullen (Lemma 3.20 in \cite{Mc1}) and Magid (Theorem 1.2 in \cite{Mag}), respectively.
nodes.statement_short: The estimates come from a nearly isometric c-filling map, via McMullen's and Magid's estimates.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.1
nodes.statement:
Let us take a neighborhood $U$ of $(
u,\infty)$ in $\mathcal A$, a neighborhood $V$ of $\sigma_{
u}$ in $AH(N,P)$ and a homeomorphism $\Phi:U 	o V$ as in the statement of Theorem ef{BromThm}. We may assume that $V \subset \Omega$. We will show below that estimates 1 and 2 are obtained if we modify $U$ sufficiently small. For $(\mu,\zeta) \in U$ with $\zeta 
e \infty$, let $$ \phi_{\mu,\zeta}:\hat M_{\mu,\zeta} 	o M_{\mu,\zeta} $$ be the $c$-filling map. To control the distortion of the map $\phi_{\mu,\zeta}$, we need to recall the notion of normalized length. Suppose that $\delta>0$ is less than the Margulis constant for hyperbolic 3-manifolds, and let $\mathbb{T}_\delta(T)$ denote the component of $\delta$-thin part of $\hat M_{\mu,\zeta}$ associated to the rank-2 cusp. We endow the boundary $\partial \mathbb{T}_\delta(T)$ of $\mathbb{T}_\delta(T)$ with the natural Euclidean metric. The marking map $\hat N 	o \hat M_{\mu,\zeta}$ induces a marking map $T 	o \partial \mathbb{T}_\delta(T)$. Via this marking, the pair of generators $b,c $ of $\pi_1(T)$ are also regarded as the pair of generators of $\pi_1(\partial \mathbb{T}_\delta(T))$. In this setting, the {\it normalized length} $L(c)$ of the free homotopy class of $c \subset \partial \mathbb{T}_\delta (T)$ is defined by $$ L(c):= rac{\mathrm{length}(c')} {\sqrt{\mathrm{Area}(\partial \mathbb{T}_\delta(T))}}, $$ where $\mathrm{length}(c')$ is the Euclidean length of the geodesic representative $c'$ of $c$ in $\partial \mathbb{T}_\delta (T)$. This $L(c)$ does not depend on the choice of $\delta$. Since $$ \hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(b)= \left( egin{array}{cc} 1 & 2 \ 0& 1 \end{array}ight) \quad 	ext{and} \quad \hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(c)=\left( egin{array}{cc} 1 & \zeta \ 0& 1 \end{array}ight), $$ the normalized length $L(c)$ can be calculated concretely as $$ L(c)= rac{|\zeta|}{\sqrt{2 \, \mathrm{Im} \,\zeta}}. $$ For any given $K>0$, we can choose the neighborhood $U$ sufficiently small so that for all $(\mu,\zeta) \in U$ with $\zeta 
e \infty$, the normalized length $L(c)$ of $c$ at the rank-$2$ cusp of $\hat M_{\mu,\zeta}$ is greater than $K$. We will show below that if we take such $K$ sufficiently large, the estimates 1 and 2 hold. We may assume that there is a uniform upper bound of $|\mu|$ for $(\mu,\zeta) \in U$. nodes.name: Recall normalized length
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\delta>0$ is less than the Margulis constant for hyperbolic 3-manifolds, and let $\mathbb{T}_\delta(T)$ denote the component of $\delta$-thin part of $\hat M_{\mu,\zeta}$ associated to the rank-2 cusp. The marking map $\hat N \to \hat M_{\mu,\zeta}$ induces a marking map $T \to \partial \mathbb{T}_\delta(T)$. Via this marking, the pair of generators $b,c $ of $\pi_1(T)$ are also regarded as the pair of generators of $\pi_1(\partial \mathbb{T}_\delta(T))$. In this setting, the {\it normalized length} $L(c)$ of the free homotopy class of $c \subset \partial \mathbb{T}_\delta (T)$ is defined by $$ L(c):=\frac{\mathrm{length}(c')} {\sqrt{\mathrm{Area}(\partial \mathbb{T}_\delta(T))}}, $$ where $\mathrm{length}(c')$ is the Euclidean length of the geodesic representative $c'$ of $c$ in $\partial \mathbb{T}_\delta (T)$. This $L(c)$ does not depend on the choice of $\delta$. Since $$ \hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(b)= \left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & 2 \\ 0& 1 \end{array}\right) \quad \text{and} \quad \hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(c)=\left(\begin{array}{cc} 1 & \zeta \\ 0& 1 \end{array}\right), $$ the normalized length $L(c)$ can be calculated concretely as $$ L(c)=\frac{|\zeta|}{\sqrt{2 \, \mathrm{Im} \,\zeta}}. $$

We can now apply a theorem of McMullen (Lemma 3.20 in \cite{Mc1}) to obtain $$ |{\mathrm{tr}}^2 (\hat \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(a))-{\mathrm{tr}}^2 ( \sigma_{\mu,\zeta}(a))|<C(R)\epsilon_1, $$ where $C(R)>0$ is a constant which depends only on $R$. nodes.name: Second estimate via Magid
nodes.statement: We next show the second estimate. Finally, multiplying $|\zeta/\lambda(\beta)|$ on both sides of (5.1) and using the estimate (5.2), we obtain $$ \left|\zeta-\frac{4\pi i}{\lambda(\beta)}\right| \le C' \frac{(\mathrm{Im} \zeta)^2}{|\zeta|^2}=\frac{C'}{2 L(c)^2} \mathrm{Im}\,\zeta<\epsilon \, \mathrm{Im}\,\zeta $$ for a given $\epsilon>0$ if $L(c)$ is large enough. nodes.name: Horizontal slice M(zeta)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal M(\zeta)$ denote the slice of $\mathcal A$ by fixing the second entry $\zeta \in \mathbb C \cup \{\infty\}$ in the product structure; that is, $$ \mathcal M(\zeta):=\{\mu \in \mathbb C : (\mu,\zeta) \in \mathcal A\}. $$

nodes.name: Basic properties of M(zeta)
nodes.statement: By definition of $\mathcal A$, one see that (i) $\mathcal M(\zeta)$ lies in $\mathcal M$ for every $\zeta$, (ii) $\mathcal M(\zeta)$ is empty if $\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta \le 0$, and that (iii) $\mathcal M(\infty)=\mathcal M$.

nodes.name: M(zeta) as intersection of translates of M
nodes.statement: It follows from Theorem \ref{BromLem} that if $\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta>0$ the set $\mathcal M(\zeta)$ can be written as \begin{eqnarray} \mathcal M(\zeta)= \bigcap_{k \in \mathbb Z}(k\zeta+\mathcal M), \end{eqnarray} where $k\zeta+\mathcal M=\{k\zeta+\mu : \mu \in \mathcal M\}$.

nodes.name: Wright's strip theorem
nodes.statement: It is known by Wright \cite{Wr} that the stripe $\{z \in \mathbb C : -1 \le \mathrm{Im}\,z \le 1\}$ does not intersect $\mathcal M$.

nodes.name: Hausdorff convergence
nodes.statement: Let $F_n \ (n \in \mathbb N),\,F_\infty$ be closed subsets in $\mathbb C$. We say that the sequence $F_n$ converges $F_\infty$ in the sense of Hausdorff if the following two conditions are satisfied: \begin{enumerate} \item For any $x_\infty \in F_\infty$, there is a sequence $x_n \in F_n$ such that $x_n \to x_\infty$. \item If there is a sequence $x_{n_j} \in F_{n_j}$ such that $x_{n_j} \to x_\infty$, then $x_\infty \in F_\infty$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Caratheodory convergence
nodes.statement: Let $\Omega_n \ (n \in \mathbb N),\,\Omega_\infty$ be open subsets in $\mathbb C$. We say that the sequence $\Omega_n$ converges to $\Omega_\infty$ in the sense of Carath\'{e}odory if the following two conditions are satisfied: \begin{enumerate} \item For any compact subset $X$ of $\Omega_\infty$, $X \subset \Omega_n$ for all large $n$. \item If there is an open subset $O$ of $\mathbb C$ and an infinite sequence $\{n_j\}_{j=1}^\infty$ such that $O \subset \Omega_{n_j}$, then $O \subset \Omega_\infty$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Hausdorff convergence is Caratheodory convergence of complements
nodes.statement: Note that closed subsets $F_n \subset \mathbb C$ converge to $F_\infty \subset \mathbb C$ in the sense of Hausdorff if and only of their complements $\mathbb C \setminus F_n$ converge to $\mathbb C \setminus F_\infty$ in the sense of Carath\'{e}odory.

nodes.name: Convergence of horizontal slices iff Im zeta_n tends to infinity
nodes.statement: Suppose that a sequence $\{\zeta_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ in $\mathbb C$ with $\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta_n>0$ converges to $\infty$ in $\hat {\mathbb C}$. nodes.name: Horocyclic and tangential convergence
nodes.statement: Suppose that a sequence $\{\lambda_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ in the right-half plane $\mathbb C_+=\{z \in \mathbb C \,|\, \mathrm{Re} \,z>0\}$ converges to $0$. We say that $\lambda_n \to 0$ \it{horocyclically} if for any $\epsilon>0$, $|\lambda_n -\epsilon|<\epsilon$ for all large $n$, and that $\lambda_n \to 0$ \it{tangentially} if there is a constant $\epsilon_0>0$ such that $|\lambda_n -\epsilon_0|>\epsilon_0$ for all $n$.
also_stated_at: We say that a sequence $\beta_n \in \mathbb C \setminus[-2,2]$ converges {\it horocyclically} to $2$ if for any disk in the right-half plane $\mathbb C_+$ touching at zero, $\lambda(\beta_n)$ are eventually contained in this disk.
On the other hand, we say that the sequence $\beta_n$ converges {\it tangentially} to $2$ if there is a disk in $\mathbb C_+$ touching at zero which does not contain any $\lambda(\beta_n)$.

nodes.name: Horocyclic/tangential via Im(2 pi i/lambda_n)

nodes.name: Geometric convergence
nodes.statement: We say that a sequence of discrete subgroups $G_n$ of ${\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)$ converges {\it geometrically} to a subgroup $G$ of ${\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)$ if $G_n$ converge to $G$ in the sense of Hausdorff as closed subsets of ${\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)$.

nodes.name: Geometric limits of cyclic groups (Jorgensen)
nodes.statement: Suppose that a sequence $B_n$ of loxodromic elements converges to $$ B=\left(\begin{array}{cc}1 & 2 \\0 & 1\end{array}\right) $$ in ${\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C)$. Let $\lambda_n$ denote the complex length of $B_n$. Then we have the following: \begin{enumerate} \item If $\lambda_n \to 0$ horocyclically, then the sequence $\langle B_n \rangle$ converges geometrically to $\langle B \rangle$. \item Suppose that $\lambda_n \to 0$ tangentially. nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.7
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\alpha \in \mathrm{int}(i \mathcal M({2\xi}))$. Then $(i\alpha,2\xi) \in \mathrm{int}(\mathcal A)$. Let $\epsilon_0>0$ be the constant in Proposition \ref{ball1} for $\nu=i\alpha$. Since $(i\alpha,2\xi) \in \mathrm{int}(\mathcal A)$, one can find $0<\epsilon<\epsilon_0$ such that $B_\epsilon(i \alpha, 2\xi) \subset \mathcal A$. Since the set $\mathcal A$ is invariant under the action $(z,w) \mapsto (z,w+2)$, we have $B_\epsilon(i \alpha, 2\xi+2m_n) \subset \mathcal A$. Let $K>0$ be the constant in Proposition \ref{ball1} for $\epsilon>0$ chosen above and $I=\mathrm{Im}(2 \xi)+1$. Since $|m_n| \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$, we have $|2\xi+2m_n|>K$ for all large $n$. Then by Proposition \ref{ball1}, we have $$ B_{\epsilon/2}(i \alpha, 2\xi+2m_n) \subset \mathcal D $$ for all large $n$. On the other hand, since the sequence $\{2\pi i/\lambda(\beta_n)-m_n\}$ converges to $\xi$ as $n \to \infty$, we have $$ \left|\frac{4\pi i}{\lambda(\beta_n)} -(2\xi+2m_n)\right| < \epsilon/4 $$ for all large $n$. Therefore $$ B_{\epsilon/4}\left(i \alpha, \frac{4\pi i}{\lambda(\beta_n)}\right) \subset \mathcal D $$ hold for all large $n$. Thus we obtain $B_{\epsilon/4}(\alpha) \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ for all large $n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.6
nodes.statement: We need to prove the following four conditions (H1), (H2), (C1) and (C2), where (H1) and (H2) are corresponding to the Hausdorff convergence and (C1) and (C2) are corresponding to the Carath\'{e}odory convergence: \begin{description} \item[(H1)] For any $\alpha \in i \mathcal M({2\xi})$ there exists a sequence $\alpha_n \in \mathcal L(\beta_n)$ such that $\alpha_n \to \alpha$. \item[(H2)] If $\alpha_{n_j} \in \mathcal L(\beta_{n_j})$ and $\alpha_{n_j} \to \alpha$ then $\alpha \in i\mathcal M({2\xi})$. \item[(C1)] For any compact subset $X \subset \mathrm{int}(i \mathcal M({2\xi}))$, $X \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ for all large $n$. \item[(C2)] If there exist an open subset $O \subset \mathbb C$ and a infinite sequence $\{n_j\}_{j=1}^\infty$ such that $O \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_{n_j}))$, then $O \subset \mathrm{int}(i\mathcal M({2\xi}))$. \end{description} Proof of (H1): For any $\alpha \in i\mathcal M({2\xi})$, there exists a sequence $\{\alpha(j)\}_{j =1}^\infty$ in the interior of $i\mathcal M({2\xi})$ such that $\alpha(j) \to \alpha$ as $j \to \infty$. It follows from Lemma \ref{tanlem} that for every $j$, there exists positive constant $N(j)$ such that $\alpha(j) \in \mathcal L(\beta_n)$ for all $n \ge N(j)$. Thus we obtain the result. To be more precise, let us choose $\{N(j)\}_{j=1}^\infty$ so that $N(j+1)>N(j)$ and $N(j) \to \infty$ as $j \to \infty$, and set $\alpha_n:=\alpha(j)$ for every $N(j) \le n < N(j)$. Since $j \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$, we obtain $\alpha_n \in \mathcal L(\beta_n)$ and $\alpha_n \to \alpha$ as $n \to \infty$. \bigskip Proof of (C1): Let $X$ be a compact subset of $\mathrm{int}(i \mathcal M({2\xi}))$. For every $\alpha \in X$, it follows from Lemma \ref{tanlem} that there exist $\epsilon(\alpha)>0$ and $N(\alpha)>0$ such that $B_{\epsilon(\alpha)}(\alpha) \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ for all $n \ge N(\alpha)$. Since $$ \bigcup_{\alpha \in X} B_{\epsilon(\alpha)}(\alpha) $$ is an open covering of the compact set $X$, we can choose finite set of points $\{\alpha_j\}_{j=1}^l \subset X$ such that $$ \bigcup_{1 \le j \le l} B_{\epsilon(\alpha_j)}(\alpha_j) $$ is also an open covering of $X$. Set $N:=\max_{1 \le j \le l}{N(\alpha_j)}$. Then $B_{\epsilon(\alpha_j)}(\alpha_j) \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ for all $n \ge N$ and all $1 \le j \le l$. Thus we obtain $X \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ for all $n \ge N$. \bigskip Proof of (H2): For simplicity, we denote $\{n_j\}$ by $\{n\}$ and assume that $\alpha_{n} \in \mathcal L(\beta_{n})$ converge to $\alpha$ as $n \to \infty$. Take $\rho_n \in AH(N,P) \cap \Omega$ such that ${\mathrm{Tr}}(\rho_n)=(\alpha_n,\beta_n)$. Since $\alpha_n \to \alpha$ and $\beta_n \to 2$, the sequence $\{\rho_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ converges algebraically to the conjugacy class of $\sigma_{i\alpha}$ in $AH(N,P)$. We may assume that the representatives of the conjugacy classes $\rho_n$, which are also denoted by $\rho_n$, converge algebraically to $\sigma_{i\alpha}$. We now consider representations $\chi_n$ of $\pi_1({\hat N})=\langle a,b,c : [b,c]=\mathit{id} \rangle$ into ${\mathrm{PSL}}(2,\mathbb C) $ defined by $$ \chi_n(a):=\rho_n(a), \quad \chi_n(b):=\rho_n(b), \quad \chi_n(c):=(\rho_n(b))^{-m_{n}}. $$ One can see form Theorem \ref{cyclic} that the sequence $\chi_n$ converges algebraically to $\chi_\infty:=\hat \sigma_{i\alpha,2\xi}$, which is defined in 4.2. We now claim that $\chi_\infty=\hat \sigma_{i\alpha,2\xi}$ is faithful and discrete. If this is true, we obtain $(i\alpha,2\xi) \in \mathcal B$. Especially we have $\mathrm{Im}\,\xi \ne 0$. It then follows from $\mathrm{Im}\,\xi \ge 0$ that $(i\alpha,2\xi) \in \mathcal A$, and thus $\alpha \in i \mathcal M({2\xi})$. Therefore we only have to show the claim above. Since $\pi_1({\hat N})$ is finitely generated and since the image $\chi_n(\pi_1({\hat N}))$ of $\chi_n$ is equal to the discrete group $\rho_n(\pi_1(N))$, it follows from the theorem due to J{\o}rgensen and Klein in \cite{JK} that $\chi_\infty(\pi_1({\hat N}))$ is discrete and that there exist group homomorphisms $$ \psi_n:\chi_\infty(\pi_1({\hat N})) \to \chi_n(\pi_1({\hat N})) $$ satisfying $\chi_n=\psi_n \circ \chi_\infty$. Now suppose for contradiction that there is a non-trivial element $g$ in $\ker \chi_\infty$. Then it must lie in $\ker \chi_n$ for all $n$. Since $\ker \chi_n$ is normally generated by a word $ b^{m_n}c$, and since the word length of $g \in \pi_1({\hat N})$ with respect to the generators $a,b,c$ is bounded, we obtain a contradiction. Thus we obtain the claim. \bigskip Proof of (C2): By the same argument as in the proof for (H2), we have $\alpha \in i\mathcal M({2\xi})$ for every $\alpha \in O$. Therefore $O \subset i\mathcal M({2\xi})$. Since $O$ is open, we have $O \subset \mathrm{int}(i\mathcal M({2\xi}))$.

It then follows from $\mathrm{Im}\,\xi \ge 0$ that $(i\alpha,2\xi) \in \mathcal A$, and thus $\alpha \in i \mathcal M({2\xi})$. Therefore we only have to show the claim above. Since $\pi_1({\hat N})$ is finitely generated and since the image $\chi_n(\pi_1({\hat N}))$ of $\chi_n$ is equal to the discrete group $\rho_n(\pi_1(N))$, it follows from the theorem due to J{\o}rgensen and Klein in \cite{JK} that $\chi_\infty(\pi_1({\hat N}))$ is discrete and that there exist group homomorphisms $$ \psi_n:\chi_\infty(\pi_1({\hat N})) \to \chi_n(\pi_1({\hat N})) $$ satisfying $\chi_n=\psi_n \circ \chi_\infty$. Now suppose for contradiction that there is a non-trivial element $g$ in $\ker \chi_\infty$. Then it must lie in $\ker \chi_n$ for all $n$. Since $\ker \chi_n$ is normally generated by a word $ b^{m_n}c$, and since the word length of $g \in \pi_1({\hat N})$ with respect to the generators $a,b,c$ is bounded, we obtain a contradiction. Thus we obtain the claim.
nodes.statement_short: H2: limit point lies in i M(2 xi)

nodes.name: Lift alpha_n to rho_n converging to sigma_{i alpha}
nodes.statement: Proof of (H2): For simplicity, we denote $\{n_j\}$ by $\{n\}$ and assume that $\alpha_{n} \in \mathcal L(\beta_{n})$ converge to $\alpha$ as $n \to \infty$. Take $\rho_n \in AH(N,P) \cap \Omega$ such that ${\mathrm{Tr}}(\rho_n)=(\alpha_n,\beta_n)$. Since $\alpha_n \to \alpha$ and $\beta_n \to 2$, the sequence $\{\rho_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ converges algebraically to the conjugacy class of $\sigma_{i\alpha}$ in $AH(N,P)$. We may assume that the representatives of the conjugacy classes $\rho_n$, which are also denoted by $\rho_n$, converge algebraically to $\sigma_{i\alpha}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift alpha_n to rho_n converging to sigma_{i alpha}

nodes.name: Define chi_n with chi_n(c)=rho_n(b)^{-m_n}

Since $\ker \chi_n$ is normally generated by a word $ b^{m_n}c$, and since the word length of $g \in \pi_1({\hat N})$ with respect to the generators $a,b,c$ is bounded, we obtain a contradiction. nodes.name: C2: same argument as H2
nodes.statement: Proof of (C2): By the same argument as in the proof for (H2), we have $\alpha \in i\mathcal M({2\xi})$ for every $\alpha \in O$. Therefore $O \subset i\mathcal M({2\xi})$. Since $O$ is open, we have $O \subset \mathrm{int}(i\mathcal M({2\xi}))$.
nodes.statement_short: C2: same argument as H2

nodes.name: Main theorem for horocyclic convergence
nodes.statement: Let $\{\beta_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence in $\mathbb C \setminus [-2,2]$ which converges to $2$ as $n \to \infty$. Suppose that $\lambda(\beta_n)$ converge horocyclically to $0$. Then we have the following: \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal L(\beta_n)$ converge to $i\mathcal M$ in the sense of Hausdorff as $n \to \infty$. \item $\mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ converge to $\mathrm{int}(i \mathcal M)$ in the sense of Carath\'{e}odory as $n \to \infty$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $\{\beta_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence in $\mathbb C \setminus [-2,2]$ which converges to $2$ as $n \to \infty$
conclusions: $\mathcal L(\beta_n)$ converge to $i\mathcal M$ in the sense of Hausdorff as $n \to \infty$
$\mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ converge to $\mathrm{int}(i \mathcal M)$ in the sense of Carath\'{e}odory as $n \to \infty$
nodes.statement_short: Under horocyclic convergence, linear slices converge to the Maskit slice iM (Hausdorff) and interiors converge (Caratheodory).
nodes.label: horo

nodes.name: Interior points persist (horocyclic case)
nodes.statement: Under the same assumption as in Theorem \ref{horo}, we have the following: For any $\alpha \in \mathrm{int}(i \mathcal M)$ there exists $\epsilon>0$ such that $B_\epsilon(\alpha) \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ for all large $n$.
assumptions: the same assumption as in Theorem \ref{horo}
conclusions: there exists $\epsilon>0$ such that $B_\epsilon(\alpha) \subset  \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ for all large $n$
nodes.label: horolem

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.9
nodes.statement: Let $\epsilon_0>0$ be the constant in Proposition \ref{ball2} for $\mu=i\alpha \in\mathrm{int}(\mathcal M)$. Let us take $0<\epsilon<\epsilon_0$ such that $B_\epsilon(i\alpha) \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal M)$. By Theorem \ref{BromLem}, one see that there exists $I>0$ such that $B_{\epsilon,I}(i\alpha) \subset \mathcal A$. Then by Proposition \ref{ball2}, if we choose $I>0$ sufficiently large, we have $B_{\epsilon/2,2I}(i \alpha) \subset \mathcal D$. Since $\lambda(\beta_n) \to 0$ horocyclically, $\mathrm{Im}(4\pi i/\lambda(\beta_n))>2I$ for all large $n$. Thus, for every $\alpha' \in B_{\epsilon/2}(\alpha)$, we have $(i\alpha', 4\pi i/\lambda(\beta_n)) \in \mathcal D$, or $(\alpha', \beta_n) \in \mathcal D_{\mathrm{tr}}$. Therefore we obtain $B_{\epsilon/2}(\alpha) \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ for all large $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 4.2 gives a tall product neighborhood in A, Proposition 5.3 transfers it to D, and horocyclic convergence puts 4 pi i/lambda(beta_n) inside it.

nodes.name: Choose eps from Proposition 5.3
nodes.statement: Let $\epsilon_0>0$ be the constant in Proposition \ref{ball2} for $\mu=i\alpha \in\mathrm{int}(\mathcal M)$. Let us take $0<\epsilon<\epsilon_0$ such that $B_\epsilon(i\alpha) \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose eps from Proposition 5.3

nodes.name: Theorem 4.2 gives B_{eps,I}(i alpha) in A
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{BromLem}, one see that there exists $I>0$ such that $B_{\epsilon,I}(i\alpha) \subset \mathcal A$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 4.2 gives B_{eps,I}(i alpha) in A

nodes.name: Proposition 5.3 gives B_{eps/2,2I} in D
nodes.statement: Then by Proposition \ref{ball2}, if we choose $I>0$ sufficiently large, we have $B_{\epsilon/2,2I}(i \alpha) \subset \mathcal D$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 5.3 gives B_{eps/2,2I} in D

nodes.name: Horocyclic convergence: Im(4 pi i/lambda) > 2I eventually
nodes.statement: Since $\lambda(\beta_n) \to 0$ horocyclically, $\mathrm{Im}(4\pi i/\lambda(\beta_n))>2I$ for all large $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Horocyclic convergence: Im(4 pi i/lambda) > 2I eventually

nodes.name: Conclude B_{eps/2}(alpha) in int L(beta_n)
nodes.statement: Thus, for every $\alpha' \in B_{\epsilon/2}(\alpha)$, we have $(i\alpha', 4\pi i/\lambda(\beta_n)) \in \mathcal D$, or $(\alpha', \beta_n) \in \mathcal D_{\mathrm{tr}}$. Therefore we obtain $B_{\epsilon/2}(\alpha) \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ for all large $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude B_{eps/2}(alpha) in int L(beta_n)

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.8
nodes.statement: The proof is almost parallel to that of Theorem \ref{tan}. We need to show the following four conditions: \begin{description} \item[(H1)] For any $\alpha \in i \mathcal M$ there exists $\alpha_n \in \mathcal L(\beta_n)$ such that $\alpha_n \to \alpha$. \item[(H2)] If $\alpha_{n_j} \in \mathcal L(\beta_{n_j})$ and $\alpha_{n_j} \to \alpha$ then $\alpha \in i\mathcal M$. \item[(C1)] For any compact subset $X$ in $\mathrm{int}(i \mathcal M)$, $X \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ for all large $n$. \item[(C2)] If there exist an open subset $O \subset \mathbb C$ and a infinite sequence $\{n_j\}_{j=1}^\infty$ such that $O \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_{n_j}))$ then $O \subset \mathrm{int}(i\mathcal M)$. \end{description} Proof of (H1): For any $\alpha \in i\mathcal M$, there exists a sequence $\alpha(j) \in \mathrm{int}(i\mathcal M)$ such that $\alpha(j) \to \alpha \ (j \to \infty)$. It follows from Lemma \ref{horolem} that for each $j$ we have $\alpha(j) \in \mathcal L(\beta_n)$ for all large $n$. Thus we obtain the claim. Proof of (C1): Let $X \subset \mathrm{int}(i \mathcal M)$ be a compact subset. For each $\alpha \in X$, it follows from Lemma \ref{horolem} that there exist $\epsilon(\alpha)>0$ and $N(\alpha)>0$ such that $B_{\epsilon(\alpha)}(\alpha) \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ for all $n \ge N(\alpha)$. Since $\bigcup_{\alpha \in X} B_{\epsilon(\alpha)}(\alpha)$ is an open covering of $X$, we may choose a finite set of points $\{\alpha_j\} \subset X$ such that $\bigcup_{j} B_{\epsilon(\alpha_j)}(\alpha_j)$ is also an open covering. Since $B_{\epsilon(\alpha_j)}(\alpha_j) \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ for all $n \ge N:=\max_j{N(\alpha_j)}$, we have $X \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ for all $n \ge N$. Proof of (H2): For simplicity we denote $\{n_j\}$ by $\{n\}$, and assume that $\alpha_{n} \in \mathcal L(\beta_{n})$ converge to $\alpha$. Take $\rho_n \in AH(N,P) \cap \Omega$ such that ${\mathrm{Tr}}(\rho_n)=(\alpha_n,\beta_n)$. Since $\alpha_n \to \alpha$, $\beta_n \to 2$, the sequence $\{\rho_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ converges to $\sigma_{i\alpha} \in R(N,P)$, and since $AH(N,P)$ is closed, we have $\sigma_{i\alpha} \in AH(N,P)$. Therefore we obtain $i\alpha \in \mathcal M$ and hence $\alpha \in i\mathcal M$. Proof of (C2): By the same argument as in (H2), we have $\alpha \in i\mathcal M$ for every $\alpha \in O$. Therefore $O \subset i\mathcal M$. Since $O$ is open, we have $O \subset \mathrm{int}(i\mathcal M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Verify H1, C1 via Lemma 6.9 and compactness; H2, C2 via closedness of AH(N,P).

nodes.statement: Proof of (H1): For any $\alpha \in i\mathcal M$, there exists a sequence $\alpha(j) \in \mathrm{int}(i\mathcal M)$ such that $\alpha(j) \to \alpha \ (j \to \infty)$. It follows from Lemma \ref{horolem} that for each $j$ we have $\alpha(j) \in \mathcal L(\beta_n)$ for all large $n$. Thus we obtain the claim.

For each $\alpha \in X$, it follows from Lemma \ref{horolem} that there exist $\epsilon(\alpha)>0$ and $N(\alpha)>0$ such that $B_{\epsilon(\alpha)}(\alpha) \subset \mathrm{int}(\mathcal L(\beta_n))$ for all $n \ge N(\alpha)$. Since $\bigcup_{\alpha \in X} B_{\epsilon(\alpha)}(\alpha)$ is an open covering of $X$, we may choose a finite set of points $\{\alpha_j\} \subset X$ such that $\bigcup_{j} B_{\epsilon(\alpha_j)}(\alpha_j)$ is also an open covering. nodes.name: H2: closedness of AH(N,P)
nodes.statement: Proof of (H2): For simplicity we denote $\{n_j\}$ by $\{n\}$, and assume that $\alpha_{n} \in \mathcal L(\beta_{n})$ converge to $\alpha$. Take $\rho_n \in AH(N,P) \cap \Omega$ such that ${\mathrm{Tr}}(\rho_n)=(\alpha_n,\beta_n)$. Since $\alpha_n \to \alpha$, $\beta_n \to 2$, the sequence $\{\rho_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ converges to $\sigma_{i\alpha} \in R(N,P)$, and since $AH(N,P)$ is closed, we have $\sigma_{i\alpha} \in AH(N,P)$. Therefore we obtain $i\alpha \in \mathcal M$ and hence $\alpha \in i\mathcal M$.
nodes.statement_short: H2: closedness of AH(N,P)

nodes.name: C2: same argument as H2
nodes.statement: Proof of (C2): By the same argument as in (H2), we have $\alpha \in i\mathcal M$ for every $\alpha \in O$. Therefore $O \subset i\mathcal M$. Since $O$ is open, we have $O \subset \mathrm{int}(i\mathcal M)$.

nodes.name: Existence of a non-locally-connected linear slice
nodes.statement: There exists $\alpha\in \mathbb C$ such that $\mathcal L(\alpha)$ is not locally connected at $2 \in \partial \mathcal L(\alpha)$; that is, $U \cap \mathcal L(\alpha)$ is disconnected for any sufficiently small neighborhood $U \subset \mathbb C$ of $2$.
conclusions: There exists $\alpha\in \mathbb C$ such that $\mathcal L(\alpha)$ is not locally connected at $2 \in \partial \mathcal L(\alpha)$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.10
nodes.statement:
The homeomorphism $F:\mathcal D_{\mathrm{tr}}^+ 	o \mathcal D$ defined in section 5.3 induces a homeomorphism from  egin{eqnarray*} \mathcal L(\alpha) \cap \mathbb C_+=\{ eta \in \mathbb C : (\alpha, eta) \in \mathcal D_{\mathrm{tr}}^+\} \end{eqnarray*} to a slice $$ \{\zeta \in \hat {\mathbb C} : (i \alpha, \zeta) \in \mathcal D\} $$ of $\mathcal D$. Since $F(\alpha,2)=(i\alpha,\infty)$, to show that $\mathcal L(\alpha)$ is not locally connected at $2$ for some $\alpha$, it suffices to show that the set $\{\zeta \in \hat {\mathbb C} : (i \alpha, \zeta) \in \mathcal D\}$ is not locally connected at $\zeta=\infty$. We will show this by using the fact observed in \cite{Br} that the vertical slice $\{\zeta \in \hat {\mathbb C} : (i \alpha, \zeta) \in \mathcal A\}$ of $\mathcal A$ is not locally connected at $\zeta=\infty$ for some $\alpha$. From the argument of Bromberg in the proof of Theorem 4.15 in \cite{Br}, there exist $\mu \in \mathrm{int}(\mathcal M)$, $\zeta \in \mathbb C$ with $\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta>0$, and $\epsilon>0$ such that $B_\epsilon(\mu,\zeta+2n)$ are contained in different connected components of $$ \{(
u,z) \in \mathcal A : |
u-\mu|<2\epsilon\} $$ for every integer $n$. By Theorem ef{BromThm}, we can take neighborhoods $U$, $W$ of $(\mu,\infty)$ in $\mathcal A$, $\mathcal D$, respectively, such that $\varphi=F \circ {\mathrm{Tr}} \circ \Phi:U 	o W$ is a homeomorphism. We may assume that $U$ is of the form $$ U=\mathcal A \cap \{(
u,z) \in \mathbb C^2 : |
u-\mu|<2\epsilon, |z|>K\}. $$ Then for all large $n$, $B_\epsilon(\mu,\zeta+2n)$ are contained in $U$, and thus contained in distinct connected components of $U$. By choosing $\epsilon>0$ sufficiently small and $K>0$ sufficiently large, we see from Proposition ef{ball1} that $B_{\epsilon/2}(\mu,\zeta+2n) \subset \mathcal D$ for all large $n$. Therefore, $B_{\epsilon/2}(\mu,\zeta+2n)$ are contained in distinct connected components of $W$ for all large $n$. Since $W \subset \mathcal D$ is a neighborhood of $(\mu,\infty)$, we see that the set $\{\zeta \in \hat {\mathbb C} : (\mu, \zeta) \in \mathcal D\}$ is not locally connected at $\zeta=\infty$. Letting $\alpha=-i\mu$, we obtain the result.
nodes.statement_short: Transfer Bromberg's non-local-connectivity of a vertical slice of A to D through varphi, using Proposition 5.2 on the separated balls.

nodes.name: F identifies L(alpha) near 2 with a vertical slice of D
nodes.statement: The homeomorphism $F:\mathcal D_{\mathrm{tr}}^+ \to \mathcal D$ defined in section 5.3 induces a homeomorphism from \begin{eqnarray*} \mathcal L(\alpha) \cap \mathbb C_+=\{\beta \in \mathbb C : (\alpha,\beta) \in \mathcal D_{\mathrm{tr}}^+\} \end{eqnarray*} to a slice $$ \{\zeta \in \hat {\mathbb C} : (i \alpha, \zeta) \in \mathcal D\} $$ of $\mathcal D$.
nodes.statement_short: F identifies L(alpha) near 2 with a vertical slice of D

nodes.name: Reduce to non-local connectivity of the vertical slice at in
nodes.statement: Since $F(\alpha,2)=(i\alpha,\infty)$, to show that $\mathcal L(\alpha)$ is not locally connected at $2$ for some $\alpha$, it suffices to show that the set $\{\zeta \in \hat {\mathbb C} : (i \alpha, \zeta) \in \mathcal D\}$ is not locally connected at $\zeta=\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to non-local connectivity of the vertical slice at infinity

nodes.name: Use Bromberg's vertical slice of A
nodes.statement: We will show this by using the fact observed in \cite{Br} that the vertical slice $\{\zeta \in \hat {\mathbb C} : (i \alpha, \zeta) \in \mathcal A\}$ of $\mathcal A$ is not locally connected at $\zeta=\infty$ for some $\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Use Bromberg's vertical slice of A

nodes.name: Bromberg: balls B_eps(mu, zeta+2n) in distinct components
nodes.statement: From the argument of Bromberg in the proof of Theorem 4.15 in \cite{Br}, there exist $\mu \in \mathrm{int}(\mathcal M)$, $\zeta \in \mathbb C$ with $\mathrm{Im}\,\zeta>0$, and $\epsilon>0$ such that $B_\epsilon(\mu,\zeta+2n)$ are contained in different connected components of $$ \{(\nu,z) \in \mathcal A : |\nu-\mu|<2\epsilon\} $$ for every integer $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Bromberg: balls B_eps(mu, zeta+2n) in distinct components

nodes.name: Take U, W with varphi a homeomorphism
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{BromThm}, we can take neighborhoods $U$, $W$ of $(\mu,\infty)$ in $\mathcal A$, $\mathcal D$, respectively, such that $\varphi=F \circ {\mathrm{Tr}} \circ \Phi:U \to W$ is a homeomorphism. We may assume that $U$ is of the form $$ U=\mathcal A \cap \{(\nu,z) \in \mathbb C^2 : |\nu-\mu|<2\epsilon, |z|>K\}. $$ Then for all large $n$, $B_\epsilon(\mu,\zeta+2n)$ are contained in $U$, and thus contained in distinct connected components of $U$.
nodes.statement_short: Take U, W with varphi a homeomorphism

nodes.name: Proposition 5.2 puts half-balls in distinct components of W
nodes.statement: By choosing $\epsilon>0$ sufficiently small and $K>0$ sufficiently large, we see from Proposition \ref{ball1} that $B_{\epsilon/2}(\mu,\zeta+2n) \subset \mathcal D$ for all large $n$. Therefore, $B_{\epsilon/2}(\mu,\zeta+2n)$ are contained in distinct connected components of $W$ for all large $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 5.2 puts half-balls in distinct components of W

nodes.name: Conclude non-local connectivity with alpha=-i mu
nodes.statement: Since $W \subset \mathcal D$ is a neighborhood of $(\mu,\infty)$, we see that the set $\{\zeta \in \hat {\mathbb C} : (\mu, \zeta) \in \mathcal D\}$ is not locally connected at $\zeta=\infty$. Letting $\alpha=-i\mu$, we obtain the result.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude non-local connectivity with alpha=-i mu

nodes.name: Fuchsian representation eta_lambda
nodes.statement: Given $\lambda>0$, we define a representation $\eta_\lambda \in R(N,P)$ by $$ \eta_\lambda(a):=\frac{1}{\sinh (\lambda/2)}\left(\begin{array}{cc} \cosh(\lambda/2) & -1 \\ -1 & \cosh(\lambda/2) \end{array}\right), \quad \eta_\lambda(b):=\left(\begin{array}{cc} e^{\lambda/2} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-\lambda/2} \end{array}\right). $$

nodes.name: Twisted Fuchsian representation eta_{lambda,tau}
nodes.statement: Given $(\lambda,\tau) \in \mathbb R_+ \times \mathbb R$, we define a fuchsian representation $\eta_{\lambda,\tau} \in R(N,P)$ by $$ \eta_{\lambda,\tau}(a):=\left(\begin{array}{cc} e^{\tau/2} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-\tau/2} \end{array}\right)\eta_{\lambda}(a), \quad \eta_{\lambda,\tau}(b) :=\eta_{\lambda}(b). $$

nodes.name: Fenchel-Nielsen map FN
nodes.statement: Now we obtain a map $$ FN:\mathbb R_+ \times \mathbb R \to R(N,P) $$ defined by $(\lambda,\tau) \mapsto \eta_{\lambda,\tau}$.

nodes.name: Fenchel-Nielsen coordinates parametrize Fuchsian space
nodes.statement: It is well-known that this map is a homeomorphism onto the space of Fuchsian representations.

nodes.name: Complex Fenchel-Nielsen coordinates
nodes.statement: By allowing the parameters $\lambda,\tau$ to be complex numbers, we obtain a map $$ FN:(\mathbb C \setminus 2\pi i \mathbb Z) \times \mathbb C \to R(N,P). $$ We say that $(\lambda,\tau)$ is the {\it complex Fenchel-Nielsen coordinates} of the representation $\eta_{\lambda,\tau}$.

nodes.name: Complex Fenchel-Nielsen coordinates on quasifuchsian space (Kourouniotis, Tan)
nodes.statement: It is known by Kourouniotis \cite{Ko} and Tan \cite{Ta} that there is an open subset of $(\mathbb C \setminus 2\pi i \mathbb Z) \times \mathbb C$ containing $\mathbb R_+ \times \mathbb R$ such that the map $FN$ induces a homeomorphism from this set onto the quasifuchsian space $MP(N,P)$.

nodes.name: Domain D_FN
nodes.statement: Let $$ \mathcal D_{FN}:=\{(\lambda,\tau) \in (\mathbb C \setminus 2\pi i \mathbb Z) \times \mathbb C : \eta_{\lambda,\tau} \in AH(N,P)\}. $$

nodes.name: Theta maps D_FN onto D_tr
nodes.statement: Since we have \begin{eqnarray*} {\mathrm{tr}}^2 \eta_{\lambda,\tau}(a) &=& 4 \coth^2 \left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right)\cosh^2\left(\frac{\tau}{2}\right), \\ {\mathrm{tr}}^2 \eta_{\lambda,\tau}(b)&=&4 \cosh^2 \left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right), \end{eqnarray*} the map $\Theta: (\mathbb C \setminus 2\pi i \mathbb Z) \times \mathbb C \to \mathbb C^2$ defined by $$ \Theta(\lambda,\tau):=\left( 2\coth \left( \frac{\lambda}{2} \right) \cosh \left( \frac{\tau}{2} \right), 2 \cosh \left( \frac{\lambda}{2} \right) \right) $$ takes $\mathcal D_{FN}$ onto $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
nodes.statement_short: The trace formulas for eta_{lambda,tau} show that Theta(lambda,tau) maps D_FN onto D_tr.

nodes.name: Fenchel-Nielsen slice L-tilde(lambda)
nodes.statement: For a given $\lambda \in \mathbb C \setminus 2\pi i \mathbb Z$, let $$ \widetilde \mathcal L(\lambda):=\{\tau \in \mathbb C: \eta_{\lambda,\tau} \in AH(N,P)\}. $$

nodes.name: Map f_lambda
nodes.statement: We define a map $f_\lambda:\mathbb C \to \mathbb C$ by $$ f_\lambda(z):=2 \coth\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right)\cosh\left(\frac{z}{2}\right) $$ so that we have $\Theta(\lambda,\tau)=(f_\lambda(\tau), 2\cosh(\lambda/2))$.

nodes.name: f_lambda maps L-tilde onto L(beta)
nodes.statement: Then the map $f_\lambda$ takes $\widetilde \mathcal L(\lambda)$ onto $\mathcal L(\beta)$ where $\beta=2\cosh (\lambda/2)$.

nodes.name: Invariance of L-tilde(lambda)
nodes.statement: Note that $\widetilde \mathcal L(\lambda)$ is $\langle z+\lambda, z+2 \pi i \rangle$-invariant, where the translation $z \mapsto z+\lambda$ corresponds to the Dehn twist about $b$.

nodes.name: Normalized slice L-hat(lambda)
nodes.statement: Let us define a map $g_\lambda:\mathbb C \to \mathbb C$ by $$ g_\lambda(z):=\frac{2}{\lambda}(z-\pi i) $$ and set $$ \widehat \mathcal L(\lambda):=g_\lambda (\widetilde \mathcal L(\lambda)) $$

nodes.name: h_lambda maps L-hat onto L(beta)
nodes.statement: Then $\widehat \mathcal L(\lambda)$ is $\langle z+2, z+4 \pi i/\lambda \rangle$-invariant and the map $$ h_\lambda(z):=f_\lambda \circ g_\lambda^{-1}(z) $$ takes zero to zero and $\widehat \mathcal L(\lambda)$ onto $\mathcal L(\beta)$, where $\beta=2\cosh(\lambda/2)$.
nodes.statement_short: L-hat(lambda) is invariant under z+2 and z+4 pi i/lambda, and h_lambda = f_lambda o g_lambda^{-1} maps it onto L(beta) fixing 0.

nodes.name: h_lambda converges to iz
nodes.statement: Since \begin{eqnarray*} h_\lambda(z) &=&2\coth\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right)\cosh\left(\frac{\lambda z}{4}+\frac{\pi i}{2}\right) \\ &=&2i \coth\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right)\sinh\left(\frac{\lambda z}{4}\right), \end{eqnarray*} one can see that if $\lambda_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, then $h_{\lambda_n}(z) \to iz$ uniformly on any compact subset of $\mathbb C$.

nodes.name: Convergence of normalized Fenchel-Nielsen slices
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\lambda_n \in \mathbb C_+, \lambda_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. \begin{enumerate} \item If $\lambda_n \to 0$ horocyclically, then $\widehat \mathcal L(\lambda_n)$ converge to $\mathcal M$ in the sense of Hausdorff, and $\mathrm{int}(\widehat \mathcal L(\lambda_n))$ converge to $\mathrm{int}(\mathcal M)$ in the sense of Carath\'{e}odory. \item Suppose that $\lambda_n \to 0$ tangentially. In addition we assume that there exist a sequence of integers $\{m_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ such that the sequence $2\pi i/\lambda_n-m_n$ converges to some $\xi \in \mathbb C$ as $n \to \infty$. Then $\widehat \mathcal L(\lambda_n)$ converge to $\mathcal M({2\xi})$ in the sense of Hausdorff, and $\mathrm{int}(\widehat \mathcal L(\lambda_n))$ converge to $\mathrm{int}(\mathcal M({2\xi}))$ in the sense of Carath\'{e}odory. \end{enumerate}
